analysis.one_liner: Replaces private campaign money in House elections with public financing funded by a corporate tax surcharge and voluntary taxpayer checkoffs.
analysis.headline: The Public Interest Campaign Reform Act was referred to two House committees in June 1996 and never received a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended large-donor financing of House campaigns. Candidates would draw from a public fund paid for by taxpayers who choose to divert part of their refund and by a small tax increase on large corporations, and would face spending limits tied to each district's median income. It also banned unregulated 'soft money' and independent attack ads in House races, and required 'stand by your ad' disclosures on television. It died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: House candidates who cannot raise large sums—challengers, third-party and independent candidates, and candidates from lower-income districts—would get public campaign money and be freed from chasing big donors. Ordinary voters would see spending limits on candidates, a ban on soft money, and clearer disclosure of who pays for ads.

how_it_helps.text: House general-election candidates would be financed from a public 'Grassroots Good Citizenship Fund,' with per-candidate amounts set by formula and paid by the Federal Election Commission, rather than by large donors [S2][S3].
Taxpayers could voluntarily designate part of their tax refund—$1 up to $10,000—to the public fund, or up to $1,000 to party committees earmarked for House candidates [S2][S3].
The fund would also be financed by raising the corporate income tax rate on taxable income above $10 million from 35% to 35.1%, with the revenue dedicated to the fund [S2][S3].
House candidates would be barred from using soft money—political funds not subject to federal contribution limits—and no one could make independent expenditures in House elections [S2][S3].

Candidates would face spending limits based on each district's median household income, with lower limits in primaries, and smaller-donor political committees would face new caps on primary contributions [S2][S3].

Television and radio campaign ads would have to show or state who paid for them, and candidate ads would carry the candidate's image with a 'takes full responsibility' statement for at least four seconds [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations with more than $10 million in taxable income would pay a 0.1 percentage point higher tax rate, with the money going to the public campaign fund. Large donors, large-donor political committees, and parties would lose their main channels for influencing House races through soft money and independent spending. Broadcast networks would have to donate prime-time airtime to publicize the fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations and big political donors

drawbacks.text: Banning independent expenditures entirely was almost certainly unconstitutional under the Supreme Court's Buckley v. Valeo line of cases protecting independent political spending; the bill itself includes a fallback in case its mandatory spending limits are struck down [S3].

Public financing would depend on voluntary taxpayer checkoffs, a mechanism that has historically drawn participation from only a small share of filers, so the fund could be underfunded and forced to pay candidates only pro rata amounts [S3].

Hard spending caps could handicap challengers who need to spend heavily to become known, potentially favoring well-known incumbents, and they would suppress all paid political speech in House races, which critics viewed as a First Amendment problem.
Allowing taxpayers to route up to $1,000 per return to party committees would give national and state parties a new public revenue stream alongside the ban on candidate soft money [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea—public financing with spending limits—directly attacks the dominance of large donors in House races, and the corporate cost is tiny (0.1 percentage point on income above $10 million). But the bill was bluntly designed: its outright ban on independent expenditures conflicts with settled Supreme Court doctrine, and its funding depends on voluntary checkoffs that may not raise enough money, in which case candidates would get reduced payments. A court-tested version of the same idea would have been stronger.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the two committees it was referred to—the House Oversight Committee and Ways and Means—from June 1996 until the Congress ended in January 1997, without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative David Obey introduced the bill on June 5, 1996, with Representatives Ron Dellums and Louise Slaughter as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Oversight Committee and, for the tax-related provisions, to the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
No further action was recorded before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the bill died in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large donors, corporations, and political committees that spend unregulated money on House races were better off, since the existing financing system continued for another Congress without spending limits, a soft-money ban, or public financing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in committees controlled by the House's Republican majority, but no member is on record opposing it.

industries.note: Corporations with taxable income above $10 million would pay a 0.1 percentage point higher rate to fund the public campaign account, and House candidates could no longer be financed through soft money or corporate-backed independent spending. The direct cost is small; the loss of influence over House elections is the real stake.

industries.industry: Large-donor PACs and big individual donors
industries.note: The bill caps large-donor committee contributions in primaries, bans soft money, and outlaws independent expenditures in House races, removing the main channels through which concentrated money reaches House campaigns.

Parties would lose soft money for House races but gain a new channel: taxpayers could designate up to $1,000 of their refund to party committees for House candidates, and parties could add up to 5% on top of each candidate's public allotment.

Networks would have to donate prime-time airtime to publicize the public fund and display 'paid for by' images in campaign ads, while spending limits would shrink the political advertising market that is a major revenue source.
Hard expenditure ceilings for general and primary elections would cap what candidates can spend on advertising and consulting in House races.
